_note: The state packets between browsers (src/net/state.ts, src/net/statesync.ts, wired in src/game/duel.ts). The match is a star with the host in the middle, so every guest's view of every other player is paid for by the host's UPLOAD, which is the smallest pipe most people have. Measured with tools/net-cost.ts over the real peer to peer path, the full packets cost the host 8.2 kB/s per guest in a 1v1 (67 kbit/s) and 37 kB/s in a battle royale squad with eleven bots (305 kbit/s), and every message rides in a packet of its own with about 90 bytes of SCTP, DTLS, UDP and IP on top of it.
_enabled: Off plays on the full packets, exactly as a build from before them: nothing is announced, so no peer sends a delta packet here and none is sent from here. ?deltas=0 in the address does the same for one browser without a rebuild.
_protocol: The version of the delta format, announced as `dp` on a player's own full packet (link.ts) and never assumed. A peer that does not announce it is sent the old full packets, so an old build and a new one still play together at the old cost. Bump this only for a change that an older decoder would get WRONG; a new field it does not know is dropped by the decoder on purpose, so adding one needs no bump.
_quantise: The step each number is rounded to before it goes on the wire, which is what turns a nine byte double into a one or two byte integer. position 0.01 is one centimetre, so a figure is drawn at most half a centimetre off on each axis (0.87 cm in the worst diagonal) from where its player is; the figures are drawn 100 ms behind, which for a running player is 70 cm, so the rounding is a hundredth of the lag that is already there. angle 0.1 is a tenth of a degree, at most 0.05 off; remote look is cosmetic here (a shot carries its own origin and direction as full floats, and the shooter claims the hit). health 1 is one hit point, which is finer than the health bar draws, and a sliver above zero is kept above zero. Nothing here rounds a number the simulation reads back: quantising happens on the way out, and the sender keeps its own full precision.
_keyframe: seconds is how often a stream sends a whole state instead of a difference, so a peer that lost the chain recovers on its own rather than drifting or freezing forever. It is also the heartbeat: a player or a bot standing still sends nothing at all between keyframes, and duel.ts drops a player it has not heard from for 10 seconds, so this has to stay well under that even across the host's relay (two streams in a row, so up to twice seconds x (1 + spread)). sentHistory and appliedHistory are how many past states each end keeps so a difference can be taken against an acknowledged state rather than the last one sent; 64 at 30 a second is a little over two seconds, which covers any round trip a playable match has. spread and phaseStep keep every stream from keyframing at the same moment: each takes a phase from its player id (phaseStep is the golden ratio, which spreads a run of ids about as evenly as a constant can) and stretches or shrinks its own interval by up to spread.
_ackHz: How often a receiver tells the sender which states it managed to apply, which is what lets the next difference be taken from a newer state (a smaller difference). An ack only names what changed since the last one. A request for a keyframe does not wait for this timer; it goes at once.
_rejoin: A guest whose connection drops mid-match (not one who leaves: a leave says goodbye) keeps their match running and tries the same code again every `retry` seconds; the host holds their seat, figure and all, for `hold` seconds and takes them back on it. The welcome gave each guest a key for their seat, so nobody else can take it. Ours, after how long every current battle royale holds a reconnecting player's place (a minute or two); a 1v1 does not hold, it ends as before.
_hitCheck: The host's check on a claimed hit (src/net/hitcheck.ts). One claim is at most a headshot of one round at the gun's nearest damage with every bonus it can carry, times margin; a gun's claim needs a shot from that player in the last shotWindow seconds (a round's flight and a round trip); the distance the shooter measured has to be within rangeSlack metres plus rangeShare of how far apart the host sees the two (its positions are a round trip stale); a swing is at most meleeMax (Gun Run's knife to the head) from within meleeRange; and a player's claims in any second are at most what the gun fires in one, times rateMargin. otherMax is a claim naming no gun (an older build's). Ours, set wide: they are there to stop a forged claim, and none of them may ever stop a real one.
_interest: The host's interest management: the states it passes a guest about a player or a bot within `near` metres of that guest go at the full rate; beyond it, at `midHz` a second, and beyond `far`, at `farHz`. The host's upload grows with the square of the lobby (tools/rehearsal.ts: 19 kB/s to each of seven guests, 1.1 Mbit/s in all, with everyone in one place), and in a battle royale most of the lobby is far from any one guest most of the time. A far figure is drawn from fewer states, which the jitter buffer takes in its stride (a gap of 100 ms at 10 a second), and nobody's own state to the host is thinned. ?interest=0 in the host's address sends everything at the full rate, for comparison.
_senderClock: Each state carries the sender's own clock (milliseconds, the low 16 bits: it wraps every 65 s, and the receiver unwraps it), and a figure is placed by when its states were SENT rather than when they arrived. Arrival times bunch and gap as the network jitters, and a figure interpolated on them runs, stalls and lurches though its player ran at one speed. The receiver maps each sender's clock onto its own through the smallest gap it has seen between the two (the least delayed state), creeping that gap up by creep seconds a second so one lucky early state does not pin it for good. The stamp rides only on a state that is sent anyway: a player standing still still costs nothing between keyframes. ?senderclock=0 in the address places figures by arrival, as before, for comparison.
_fast: The delta packets and their acks ride a second data channel on the same connection, unordered and never resent (a negotiated channel both ends open with the same id, so no signalling; an older build never opens it, the channel never pairs, and everything goes on the reliable one as before). On the reliable, ordered channel one lost packet held every later state behind it until it was resent, which is a stall for every figure at once; the delta format was built for loss (a difference from an acknowledged state, a keyframe every couple of seconds, a late part dropped as stale), so a lost state now costs only itself. id is the channel's number; `buffered` is how much may wait in it before a state goes on the reliable channel instead. Everything else (shots, hits, downs, the full packets an older build reads) stays reliable and ordered. ?loss=P on the local transport drops P of these and delivers the rest out of order, for the tests.
_buffer: How far behind a friend's figure is drawn: never less than min seconds, and otherwise as far as it takes to always have a state on each side of the moment it draws. What decides that is, as each state arrives, how long it has been since the time of the one before: a figure drawn less far behind than that has run out of states and stands still until the next comes in. The worst of it lately is kept (each new state keeps `keep` of the old worst: 0.99 is about three seconds of memory at 30 a second), the delay grows toward it at `grow` a second and shrinks at `shrink` (a stall is worse than a little extra delay, and a delay that jumped would jump the figure), and max caps it for a connection so bad a late figure is worse than a stuttering one. min is the 100 ms this used to be for everyone. Past the newest state (a burst of lost ones), the figure carries on along its last motion for up to `extrapolate` seconds rather than freezing, and holds after that.
